claim: CRISPR/Cas9 can be used for precise genetic knock-in of epitope tags into endogenous genes.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 can be used for precise genetic knock-in of epitope tags into endogenous genes, simplifying experimental analysis of protein function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general capability of the CRISPR/Cas9 system.

claim: Cas9-assisted epitope tagging in primary mammalian cell cultures is often inefficient and reliant on plasmid-based selection strategies.
source: However, Cas9-assisted epitope tagging in primary mammalian cell cultures is often inefficient and reliant on plasmid-based selection strategies.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods in the abstract.

claim: Co-delivery of Cas9 protein pre-complexed with two-part synthetic modified RNAs (annealed crRNA:tracrRNA) and single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) repair templates achieves improved knock-in efficiencies of diverse tags (V5, 3XFLAG, Myc, HA).
source: Here, we demonstrate improved knock-in efficiencies of diverse tags (V5, 3XFLAG, Myc, HA) using co-delivery of Cas9 protein pre-complexed with two-part synthetic modified RNAs (annealed crRNA:tracrRNA) and single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) repair templates.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Knock-in efficiencies of ~5–30% were achieved without selection in embryonic stem (ES) cells, neural stem (NS) cells, and brain-tumor-derived stem cells.
source: Knock-in efficiencies of ~5–30%, were achieved without selection in embryonic stem (ES) cells, neural stem (NS) cells, and brain-tumor-derived stem cells.
evidence: This quantitative result is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 1-3.

claim: Biallelic-tagged clonal lines were readily derived using the csRNP method.
source: Biallelic-tagged clonal lines were readily derived and used to define Olig2 chromatin-bound interacting partners.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: Olig2 chromatin-bound interacting partners were defined using biallelic-tagged clonal lines.
source: Biallelic-tagged clonal lines were readily derived and used to define Olig2 chromatin-bound interacting partners.
evidence: This application is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: A 96-well format pipeline enabled V5-tagging of 60 different transcription factors.
source: Using our novel web-based design tool, we established a 96-well format pipeline that enabled V5-tagging of 60 different transcription factors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The human protein atlas has performed systematic characterisation of antibodies against native proteins.
source: Large-scale projects, such as the human protein atlas, have performed systematic characterisation of antibodies against native proteins (Thul et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Thul et al., 2017.

claim: There are inherent difficulties in discovering, validating and distributing high-quality antibodies that cover all species and key applications.
source: However, there are inherent difficulties in discovering, validating and distributing high-quality antibodies that cover all species and key applications (e.g. immunoblotting, immunoprecipitation, ChIP-Seq and immunocytochemistry).
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge in the field.

claim: Epitope tagging involves the fusion of small peptide-coding sequences to a protein of interest (e.g. 3XFLAG, HA, V5, and Myc).
source: A complementary strategy is to use epitope tagging: the fusion of small peptide-coding sequences to a protein of interest (e.g. 3XFLAG, HA, V5, and Myc) (Jarvik and Telmer, 1998).
evidence: This is a definition cited from Jarvik and Telmer, 1998.

claim: Plasmid-driven cDNA overexpression creates artificially high-protein levels.
source: In contrast to plasmid-driven cDNA overexpression, which creates artificially high-protein levels, the knock-in of small epitope tags to endogenous genes provides physiologically relevant levels.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of overexpression approaches.

claim: Knock-in of small epitope tags to endogenous genes provides physiologically relevant protein levels.
source: In contrast to plasmid-driven cDNA overexpression, which creates artificially high-protein levels, the knock-in of small epitope tags to endogenous genes provides physiologically relevant levels.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the epitope tagging approach.

claim: Epitope tagging has been a key tool in yeast studies, resulting in global characterization of core protein complexes and their extensive interaction networks.
source: This has been a key tool in yeast studies, resulting in global characterization of core protein complexes and their extensive interaction networks (Gavin et al., 2006; Krogan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Gavin et al., 2006 and Krogan et al., 2006.

claim: Epitope tagging has not been widely adopted in mammalian cells, primarily due to the poor efficiency of homologous recombination (HR).
source: However, to date this approach has not been widely adopted in mammalian cells, primarily due to the poor efficiency of homologous recombination (HR).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation explaining why epitope tagging is not widely used in mammalian cells.

claim: Formation of a site-specific DNA double-strand break (DSBs) will massively enhance HR-mediated repair.
source: Formation of a site-specific DNA double-strand break (DSBs), will massively enhance HR-mediated repair.
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism in genome editing.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 was uncovered as a form of microbial adaptive immunity.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 was uncovered as a form of microbial adaptive immunity (Bhaya et al., 2011) that has been repurposed for genome editing in mammalian cells (Cong et al., 2013; Doudna and Charpentier, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Bhaya et al., 2011.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 has been repurposed for genome editing in mammalian cells.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 was uncovered as a form of microbial adaptive immunity (Bhaya et al., 2011) that has been repurposed for genome editing in mammalian cells (Cong et al., 2013; Doudna and Charpentier, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Cong et al., 2013 and Doudna and Charpentier, 2014.

claim: Cas9 is an RNA-guided endonuclease that binds complementary DNA via formation of a 20 bp RNA:DNA heteroduplex.
source: Cas9 is an RNA-guided endonuclease that binds complementary DNA via formation of a 20 bp RNA:DNA heteroduplex.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism of Cas9.

claim: Stable binding of Cas9/gRNA complex at the target site leads to activation of nuclease domains and formation of a double-stranded DNA break (DSB).
source: Stable binding of Cas9/gRNA complex at the target site leads to activation of nuclease domains and formation of a double-stranded DNA break (DSB) (Jinek et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Jinek et al., 2014.

claim: DSBs are predominantly repaired through the error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway, resulting in insertion or deletion mutations (indels).
source: DSBs are predominantly repaired through the error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway, resulting in insertion or deletion mutations (indels) (Sander and Joung, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Sander and Joung, 2014.

claim: HR-mediated repair occurs at lower frequencies than NHEJ.
source: Alternatively, at lower frequencies HR-mediated repair will occur.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of DNA repair pathways.

claim: Successful knock-in of tags requires co-delivery of three ingredients to mammalian cells: the Cas9 protein, a guide RNA, and a donor repair template.
source: Successful knock-in of tags, therefore, requires co-delivery of three ingredients to the mammalian cells: the Cas9 protein, a guide RNA, and a donor repair template (i.e. single or double-stranded DNA encoding the tag or reporter with homology arms).
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for CRISPR-mediated knock-in.

claim: CRISPR components are typically delivered via transient plasmid transfection or viral vectors.
source: These CRISPR components are typically delivered via transient plasmid transfection or viral vectors.
evidence: This is stated as a common practice in the field.

claim: Production of tailored plasmids for each component can be tedious and time-consuming.
source: Despite the successes of current approaches (Dalvai et al., 2015; Savic et al., 2015; Mikuni et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2017), it is clear that many bottlenecks restrict widespread applications; (i) Production of tailored plasmids for each component can be tedious and time-consuming;
evidence: This is stated as a bottleneck of current approaches.

claim: Plasmid-based selection strategies introduce additional regulatory elements that can disrupt normal regulatory processes.
source: (ii) Plasmid-based selection strategies introduce additional regulatory elements that can disrupt normal regulatory processes;
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of plasmid-based approaches.

claim: Plasmid DNA can randomly integrate in the genome causing insertional mutagenesis or increasing risks of off-target cleavage.
source: (iii) Plasmid DNA, either Cas9/gRNA expression vectors or targeting vectors, can randomly integrate in the genome causing insertional mutagenesis or increasing risks of off-target cleavage (Kim et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2015);
evidence: This is cited from Kim et al., 2014 and Liang et al., 2015.

claim: Current strategies are often not readily scalable to enable routine exploration of large numbers of genes.
source: (iv) current strategies are often not readily scalable to enable routine exploration of large numbers of genes;
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current approaches.

claim: Recovery of biallelic clonal lines is inefficient with current strategies.
source: (v) recovery of biallelic clonal lines is inefficient.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current approaches.

claim: Improved efficiencies of CRISPR editing in mammalian cells have been demonstrated using recombinant Cas9 protein.
source: Improved efficiencies of CRISPR editing in mammalian cells have been demonstrated using recombinant Cas9 protein (Kim et al., 2014; Ramakrishna et al., 2014; Bressan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Kim et al., 2014; Ramakrishna et al., 2014; Bressan et al., 2017.

claim: Cas9 protein is complexed with in vitro-transcribed (IVT) RNA to produce a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex that can be delivered into cells.
source: Cas9 protein is complexed with in vitro-transcribed (IVT) RNA, to produce a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex that can be then delivered into cells.
evidence: This is a description of the RNP method.

claim: RNPs are short-lived and cleared by cells within 24–48 hr, reducing the risk of both formation of mosaic clones or off-target cleavage.
source: The RNPs are short-lived and cleared by cells within 24–48 hr, reducing the risk of both formation of mosaic clones or off-target cleavage (Kim et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2014; Zuris et al., 2015; Cameron et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Kim et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2014; Zuris et al., 2015; Cameron et al., 2017.

claim: RNP-assisted methods have mainly been used for gene knock-out.
source: However, RNP-assisted methods have mainly been used for gene knock-out (Kim et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2015), incorporation of point mutations (Ma et al., 2017; Rivera-Torres et al., 2017), or knock-in of restriction enzyme sites (Lin et al., 2014; Schumann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources describing the applications of RNP methods.

claim: RNP with in vitro-transcribed (IVT) sgRNAs has been used for CRISPR epitope tagging, yet the efficiencies in the absence of selection are highly variable.
source: We and others have recently made use of RNP with in vitro-transcribed (IVT) sgRNAs for CRIPSR epitope tagging (Bressan et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2017), yet the efficiencies in the absence of selection are highly variable, and this approach cannot be scaled.
evidence: This is cited from Bressan et al., 2017 and Liang et al., 2017, and states a limitation.

claim: Chemically modified ~100 nt-long sgRNAs can be synthesised but are prohibitively expensive.
source: To avoid IVT, chemically modified ~100 nt-long sgRNAs can be synthesised (Hendel et al., 2015); however, these are prohibitively expensive, limiting applications.
evidence: This is cited from Hendel et al., 2015 and states a limitation.

claim: A two-part, chemically synthesised, short target-specific crRNA plus a longer generic tracrRNA is cheaper and has better performance than full-length sgRNAs.
source: Alternatively, a two-part, chemically synthesised, short target-specific crRNA plus a longer generic tracrRNA can be used. This is cheaper (only the crRNA needs to be resynthesised for new targets) and has better performance (Aida et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Aida et al., 2015 and Anderson et al., 2015.

claim: Base, backbone and end modifications of cr/tracrRNAs have advanced the dual-RNA approach.
source: This 'dual-RNA' approach has been advanced further by 'base, backbone and end' modifications of cr/tracrRNAs (Rahdar et al., 2015; Kelley et al., 2016) and also by the use of shorter and more effective modified cr/tracrRNAs (Jacobi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Rahdar et al., 2015; Kelley et al., 2016; and Jacobi et al., 2017.

claim: Modified synthetic cr/tracrRNAs are resistant to nuclease digestion, limit cellular immune responses, have greater stability, and provide enhanced targeting efficiency.
source: Modified synthetic cr/tracrRNAs are resistant to nuclease digestion, limit cellular immune responses, have greater stability, and therefore provide enhanced targeting efficiency (Jacobi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Jacobi et al., 2017.

claim: The csRNA-based RNP (csRNP) gave a >4-fold increase in V5 knock-in efficiency for Olig2 compared to IVT sgRNA.
source: The csRNA-based RNP (csRNP) gave a >4-fold and >10-fold increase in V5 knock-in efficiency for Olig2 and Sox2, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The csRNA-based RNP (csRNP) gave a >10-fold increase in V5 knock-in efficiency for Sox2 compared to IVT sgRNA.
source: The csRNA-based RNP (csRNP) gave a >4-fold and >10-fold increase in V5 knock-in efficiency for Olig2 and Sox2, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Improved knock-in efficiencies were obtained using an independent cell line (glioma-initiating neural stem cells; termed GNS).
source: Improved knock-in efficiencies were also obtained using an independent cell line (glioma-initiating neural stem cells; termed GNS) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PCR genotyping and Sanger sequencing confirmed in-frame and error-free insertion of V5 tag sequence at the C-terminus of Olig2 and Sox2 loci.
source: PCR genotyping and Sanger sequencing confirmed in-frame and error-free insertion of V5 tag sequence at the C-terminus of Olig2 and Sox2 loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: V5-positive cells all displayed the anticipated nuclear localisation and levels with no indication of non-specific expression.
source: V5-positive cells all displayed the anticipated nuclear localisation and levels with no indication of non-specific expression.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the immunocytochemistry data.

claim: Similar rates of knock-in (15–21%) were observed across all four tags (V5, HA, 3XFLAG, Myc) for Sox2.
source: Nevertheless, we observed similar rates of knock-in (15–21%) across all four tags for Sox2 (Figure 1E; Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: An independent adult NS cell culture gave similar knock-in efficiency results (9–15% knock-in efficiency).
source: An independent adult NS cell culture also gave similar results (9–15% knock-in efficiency, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sox3, Sox8, and Sox9 had knock-in efficiencies of 30%, 14% and 26%, respectively.
source: We found that Sox3, Sox8, and Sox9 – three Sox family members that are expressed in NS cells – had knock-in efficiencies of 30%, 14% and 26%, respectively (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Two different tags (Sox2: HA tag; and Olig2: V5 tag) could be simultaneously knocked-in in the same cells using a single transfection (4% double-positive cells).
source: Furthermore, we could simultaneously knock-in two different tags (Sox2: HA tag; and Olig2: V5 tag) in the same cells using a single transfection (4% double-positive cells, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Four out of eleven correctly targeted Sox2-V5 clones had successfully integrated the V5 tag sequence at both alleles (30% of V5-positive clones).
source: Of these four had successfully integrated the V5 tag sequence at both alleles (30% of V5-positive clones) (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 2.

claim: High frequencies of bi-allelic knock-in were obtained for Sox3-V5 (62.5%).
source: High frequencies of bi-allelic knock-in were also obtained for Sox3-V5 (62.5%).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Table 2.

claim: Several biallelic knock-in lines were derived from mouse GNS cells (IENS): Sox2, Sox3, Sox8 and Sox9 (7%, 26%, 57%, and 15% biallelic knock-in of V5-positive clones, respectively).
source: We also derived several biallelic knock-in lines from another independent cell line (IENS, mouse GNS cells): Sox2, Sox3, Sox8 and Sox9 (7%, 26%, 57%, and 15% biallelic knock-in of V5-positive clones, respectively) (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 2.

claim: Mouse ES cells (E14Tg2a) were tagged at similar level of efficiency to NS cells for Sox2, Sox3, Ctcf, Pou3f1, and Ezh2 (knock-in efficiency range 6–11%).
source: In each case, we found that mouse ES cells (E14Tg2a) were tagged at similar level of efficiency to the NS cells (knock-in efficiency range 6–11%, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Non-expressed genes (Sox9, Pou3f2, and Pou3f3) can be successfully tagged in ES cells without deploying any selection strategies or plasmids.
source: Thus, non-expressed genes can be successfully tagged in ES cells, without deploying any selection strategies or plasmids.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Upon neural lineage differentiation of ES cells, a proportion of Nestin-expressing neural rosettes were V5-positive for Sox9, Pou3f2, and Pou3f3 (10.5%, 20%, and 11.8%, respectively).
source: However, for each of these genes, upon neural lineage differentiation of the ES cells, we noted a proportion of the Nestin-expressing neural rosettes that were V5-positive; 10.5%, 20%, and 11.8% for Sox9, Pou3f2, and Pou3f3, respectively (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: V5 knock-in was successfully demonstrated in human ES cells for SOX2.
source: We also assessed csRNP-based tagging in human ES cells. V5 knock-in was successfully demonstrated in human ES cells for SOX2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Human GBM-derived cells were successfully tagged for OLIG2, SOX2, and SOX9 genes (15–70% efficiency).
source: We also tested human GBM-derived cells for OLIG2, SOX2, and SOX9 genes (15–70% efficiency) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The distance of the DSB to the insertion site influences the frequency of successful HR.
source: Previous studies have indicated that the distance of the DSB to the insertion site influences the frequency of successful HR (Bialk et al., 2015; Paquet et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Bialk et al., 2015; Paquet et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2017.

claim: By PCR genotyping, both proximal and distal gRNAs could result in successful tagging in the majority of cases; 30/50 genes (60%) for proximal DSB and 27/50 for the distal DSB (54%).
source: By PCR genotyping, we found that both proximal and distal gRNAs could result in successful tagging in the majority of cases; 30/50 genes (60%) for proximal DSB and 27/50 for the distal DSB (54%) (Figure 4—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figure supplements.

claim: There is a consistent trend towards increased tagging efficiency for the most proximal cut site.
source: Importantly, by comparing the efficiency of tagging for these seven genes, we noted a consistent trend towards increased tagging efficiency for the most proximal cut site.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data in Figure 4.

claim: Sox3 showed 18% and 5% knock-in efficiency for proximal and distal gRNAs, respectively.
source: For example, Sox3 showed 18% and 5% knock-in efficiency, for proximal and distal gRNAs, respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For four genes (Sox9, Foxj3, Fok1 and Foxk2), the distal gRNA did not work, whereas the proximal gRNA facilitated high knock-in efficiency.
source: For four genes (Sox9, Foxj3, Fok1 and Foxk2), the distal gRNA did not work, whereas the proximal gRNA facilitated high knock-in efficiency (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There were no genes for which the more distal gRNA worked better than the proximal gRNA.
source: There were no genes for which the more distal gRNA worked better than the proximal gRNA.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Proximity of DSB to the stop codon influences the efficiency of knock-in.
source: These results suggest proximity of DSB to the stop codon influences the efficiency of knock-in.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Sox2 tagging gave consistent V5 knock-in efficiency across the 96-well plate (10.5 ± 2.5%).
source: Sox2 tagging was used as a positive control in six wells; these gave consistent V5 knock-in efficiency across the plate, confirming no 'edge-effects' during the procedure (10.5 ± 2.5%) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For the first 96-well plate, 30 out of 90 TFs were positive for V5 ICC with typical knock-in efficiencies ranging from 6% to 29%.
source: Remarkably, for the first 96-well plate, 30 out of 90 TFs were positive for V5 ICC with typical knock-in efficiencies ranging from 6% to29% (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: A second 96-well plate with distinct TFs showed similar knock-in efficiency (5%–38%), with 31 out of 95 TFs positive for V5 ICC.
source: A second 96-well plate with distinct TFs showed similar knock-in efficiency (5%–38%), with 31 out of 95 TFs positive for V5 ICC (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: ~30% of genes were successfully tagged at the first attempt with good knock-in efficiency.
source: Thus, ~30% of genes were successfully tagged at the first attempt with good knock-in efficiency (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Two of the V5-positive TFs- Cbfb and Ybx1, showed nucleocytoplasmic localisation.
source: Interestingly, two of the V5-positive TFs- Cbfb and Ybx1, showed nucleocytoplasmic localisation (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: RIME analysis showed high enrichment of the bait protein Olig2 and subunits of SWI/SNF complexes and histone deacetylases (HDACs) in the pull-down complexes.
source: RIME analysis showed high enrichment of the bait protein Olig2 (Figure 7A) and subunits of SWI/SNF complexes and histone deacetylases (HDACs) in the pull-down complexes (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A and source data.

claim: Physical interaction of Olig2 and SWI/SNF complex has been previously reported and this interaction is essential for oligodendrocyte differentiation.
source: Physical interaction of Olig2 and SWI/SNF complex has been previously reported and this interaction is essential for oligodendrocyte differentiation (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Yu et al., 2013.

claim: HDACs have a known functional role in Olig2 function during development.
source: HDACs have a known functional role in Olig2 function during development.
evidence: This is stated as known information.

claim: ChIP-SICAP analysis showed strong enrichment of Olig2 and core histone proteins suggesting specific pull-down of chromatin fragments bound by Olig2 TF.
source: ChIP-SICAP analysis showed strong enrichment of Olig2 and core histone proteins suggesting specific pull-down of chromatin fragments bound by Olig2 TF (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Two other oligodendrocyte lineage transcription factors, Olig1 and Olig3, were detected among the most enriched proteins in ChIP-SICAP analysis.
source: Noteworthy, two other oligodendrocyte lineage transcription factors, Olig1 and Olig3, were detected among the most enriched proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the ChIP-SICAP analysis.

claim: Sets of genes regulated by various Olig proteins have a partial overlap.
source: Earlier studies reported that sets of genes regulated by various Olig proteins have a partial overlap (Ligon et al., 2007; Meijer et al., 2012), explaining co-occupation of the same DNA-sites as shown by these data.
evidence: This is cited from Ligon et al., 2007 and Meijer et al., 2012.

claim: Two other members of the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) family, Npas3 and Tcf4, were detected in ChIP-SICAP analysis.
source: Furthermore, we detected two other members of the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) family: Npas3 and Tcf4.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the ChIP-SICAP analysis.

claim: bHLH transcription factors are known to form heterodimers with other bHLH proteins on chromatin.
source: The bHLH transcription factors are known to form heterodimers with other bHLH proteins on chromatin (Massari and Murre, 2000) and the presence of Npas3 and Tcf4 may be explained by their direct physical interaction (Figure 7B; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is cited from Massari and Murre, 2000.

claim: Both Npas3 and Tcf4 have been reported to be involved in CNS development.
source: Both Npas3 and Tcf4 have been reported to be involved in CNS development (Shin and Kim, 2013; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Shin and Kim, 2013 and Chen et al., 2016.

claim: A recent study reported interactions of Olig2, Tcf4 and Npas3 in mouse neural stem cells by FLAG-affinity purification.
source: Interestingly, a recent study reporting interactions of Olig2, Tcf4 and Npas3 in mouse neural stem cells by FLAG-affinity purification (Moen et al., 2017) allowed us to correlate interactomes of all the three bHLH proteins with our data.
evidence: This is cited from Moen et al., 2017.

claim: Tcf4 and Npas3 co-localise with Olig2 on chromatin, suggesting a functional interaction.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that Tcf4 and Npas3 co-localise with Olig2 on chromatin, suggesting a functional interaction.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ChIP-SICAP data.

claim: Three known interactors of Olig2 (Cul3, Smarca4 and Sox8) were detected in the flow-through of the streptavidin enrichment.
source: Furthermore, composition of identified proteins correlates with previous findings: we detected three known interactors of Olig2 (Cul3, Smarca4 and Sox8 (BioGRID, Intact)) and 55 other proteins reported to co-precipitate with Olig2 (Moen et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated as a result and cited from BioGRID, Intact, and Moen et al., 2017.

claim: 55 other proteins reported to co-precipitate with Olig2 were detected in the flow-through of the streptavidin enrichment.
source: Furthermore, composition of identified proteins correlates with previous findings: we detected three known interactors of Olig2 (Cul3, Smarca4 and Sox8 (BioGRID, Intact)) and 55 other proteins reported to co-precipitate with Olig2 (Moen et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated as a result and cited from Moen et al., 2017.

claim: dsDNA with larger homology arms were more effective in mCherry knock-in.
source: We found that dsDNA with larger homology arms were more effective in mCherry knock-in (Figure 8B), although homology arms as small as 100 bp showed ~0.29% cells positive for mCherry in the bulk populations.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Homology arms as small as 100 bp showed ~0.29% cells positive for mCherry in the bulk populations.
source: We found that dsDNA with larger homology arms were more effective in mCherry knock-in (Figure 8B), although homology arms as small as 100 bp showed ~0.29% cells positive for mCherry in the bulk populations.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: mCherry knock-in at Olig2 and Foxg1 loci achieved 0.34% and 0.11% efficiency, respectively.
source: We next tested mCherry knock-in at Olig2 and Foxg1 loci and achieved 0.34% and 0.11% efficiency, respectively (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Live-imaging of mCherry-sorted populations for Sox2, Olig2, and Foxg1 showed the expected localisation and levels of fusion proteins in NS cells.
source: Live-imaging of mCherry-sorted populations for the three genes (Sox2, Olig2, and Foxg1) showed the expected localisation and levels of fusion proteins in NS cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The csRNP method can be used for knock-in of fluorescent reporters in NS cells.
source: Together, these results show that our csRNP method can be used for knock-in of fluorescent reporters in NS cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mCherry knock-in experiments.

claim: Use of Cas9 recombinant protein is critical for achieving significant enhancement in knock-in efficiency when combined with synthetic modified RNAs.
source: Use of Cas9 recombinant protein is critical. We found that when combined with synthetic modified RNAs significant enhancement in the efficiency is possible.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion.

claim: The method is faster and more reliable compared to plasmid-based strategies.
source: This was achieved using faster and more reliable method – compared to plasmid-based strategies.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method in the Discussion.

claim: Primary mammalian stem cell lines are readily amenable to RNP engineering, without the need for plasmid production, or prior genetic manipulation of the host cell lines.
source: Importantly, we showed primary mammalian stem cell lines are readily amenable to RNP engineering, without the need for plasmid production, or prior genetic manipulation of the host cell lines.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage in the Discussion.

claim: Assembly of RNPs with csRNAs is simple and requires only ~30 min hands-on-time.
source: Assembly of RNPs with csRNAs is simple and requires only ~30 min hands-on-time; this compared favourably to IVT reactions, which require multiple steps, are time-consuming, and result in variable quality of gRNAs.
evidence: This is stated as a practical advantage in the Discussion.

claim: IVT reactions require multiple steps, are time-consuming, and result in variable quality of gRNAs.
source: Assembly of RNPs with csRNAs is simple and requires only ~30 min hands-on-time; this compared favourably to IVT reactions, which require multiple steps, are time-consuming, and result in variable quality of gRNAs.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of IVT methods in the Discussion.

claim: csRNA reagents are stable at −20°C for many months.
source: In our hands, these reagents are stable at −20o C for many months, and is particularly convenient when re-used across a range of cell types.
evidence: This is stated as a practical observation in the Discussion.

claim: Use of the custom synthetic cr/tracrRNAs with their modified backbone and protected ends shields the RNA from cellular RNases.
source: Perhaps more importantly, use of the custom synthetic cr/tracrRNAs with their modified backbone and protected ends, shields the RNA from cellular RNases.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism explaining improved performance in the Discussion.

claim: Greatly reduced toxicity was found with csRNP compared to IVT sgRNA and plasmids-based delivery methods.
source: We found greatly reduced toxicity – one of the key advantages of the csRNP over IVT sgRNA and plasmids-based delivery methods.
evidence: This is stated as an observed advantage in the Discussion.

claim: Clonal knock-in lines were routinely generated in a time-frame of 4–6 weeks.
source: We routinely generated clonal knock-in lines in a time-frame of 4–6 weeks.
evidence: This is stated as a practical outcome in the Discussion.

claim: RNP complexes target both copies of the genes at high frequency, enabling facile isolation of bi-allelic knock-in clones.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Liang et al., 2015), we found that RNP complexes target both copies of the genes at high frequency, enabling facile isolation of bi-allelic knock-in clones.
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with prior work, cited from Liang et al., 2015.

claim: C-terminus tagging can potentially compromise protein function, localisation or levels in the edited cells.
source: Foremost, inevitably there is a risk that C-terminus tagging can potentially compromise protein function, localisation or levels in the edited cells.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat in the Discussion.

claim: Not all proteins will be amenable to tagging.
source: Not all proteins will be amenable to tagging.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the Discussion.

claim: PAM-strand (non-complementary strand) for donor DNA synthesis is less likely to be cut by Cas9 complex.
source: In this study, we used PAM-strand (non-complementary strand) for donor DNA synthesis, which is less likely to be cut by Cas9 complex (Gasiunas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Gasiunas et al., 2012.

claim: For symmetrical PAM ssODNs, both strands are equally effective for knock-in.
source: We have not compared PAM versus non-PAM donor DNA strands for knock-in efficiency although a recent report suggests that for symmetrical PAM ssODNs, both strands are equally effective for knock-in (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Liang et al., 2017.

claim: A higher HDR rate is achieved with guide RNAs that cut near the insertion site.
source: Previous findings have reported a higher HDR rate with the guide RNAs that cut near the insertion site (Bialk et al., 2015; Paquet et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Bialk et al., 2015; Paquet et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2017.

claim: Lower knock-in efficiency achieved with distal-cutting gRNAs could be attributed to 'partial HDR' events.
source: Lower knock-in efficiency achieved with the distal-cutting gRNAs could be attributed to 'partial HDR' events (Guo et al., 2018), which are not detectable in our ICC end-point assays.
evidence: This is cited from Guo et al., 2018 as a possible explanation.

claim: The average size of CRISPR/Cas9-induced indels in mammalian cells has been reported to be around 1–5 bp.
source: The average size of CRISPR/Cas9-induced indels in mammalian cells has been reported to be around 1–5 bp (Paquet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Paquet et al., 2016.

claim: It is recommended to design guide RNAs in the 3'UTR, preferably cutting 8–15 bp downstream of stop codon, to avoid interfering with the stop codon.
source: We therefore recommend designing guide RNAs in the 3'UTR, preferably cutting 8–15 bp downstream of stop codon, to avoid interfering with the stop codon.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on the findings in the Discussion.

claim: The pipeline is fully scalable and does not require sophisticated tools, expertise, or know-how.
source: The pipeline that emerges is fully scalable and does not require sophisticated tools, expertise, or know-how.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the developed pipeline in the Discussion.

claim: The whole pipeline from obtaining the reagents to imaging data was accomplished within three weeks.
source: It was possible to generate such data with relatively little labour investment, and the whole pipeline from obtaining the reagents to imaging data was accomplished within three weeks.
evidence: This is stated as a practical outcome in the Discussion.

claim: Tag-specific antibodies work universally across different cell types and species.
source: Because tag-specific antibodies work universally across different cell types and species, this approach should allow cross-species comparisons and will also complement existing efforts to develop and characterise native antibodies.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of epitope tagging in the Discussion.

claim: Tagging of DNA-binding proteins will allow comprehensive genome-wide binding sites via ChIP-Seq for key transcription factors, chromatin-modifying enzymes, and other gene regulatory proteins.
source: Furthermore, tagging of DNA-binding proteins will allow us to generate comprehensive genome-wide binding sites via ChIP-Seq for key transcription factors, chromatin-modifying enzymes, and other gene regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application in the Discussion.

claim: csRNP is highly effective for gene knockout studies.
source: Although not a focus of the current study, we also find that csRNP is highly effective for gene knockout studies (Pollard laboratory, unpublished and (Jacobi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an additional finding, with citation to Jacobi et al., 2017.
